segments.narration_text:
December 13, 2001. Gunmen storm India's Parliament in New Delhi. More than a dozen people die, including the attackers. India blamed two Pakistan-based groups: Lashkar-e-Taiba, and Jaish-e-Mohammed.

What followed was the largest military build-up on the subcontinent in decades. India called it Operation Parakram. By January 2002, around half a million Indian troops were massed on the border. Pakistan answered with hundreds of thousands of its own. Two nuclear-armed neighbours stood face to face for ten months.

The standoff eased only after Pakistan's president, Pervez Musharraf, pledged under American pressure to end cross-border infiltration. Two years after the runway, the group founded by one of the three freed men had been blamed for bringing two armies to the edge.

segments.narration_text:
Omar Sheikh was born in Britain. He studied at the London School of Economics. Then, in 1994, he was arrested in India over the kidnapping of Western tourists. The aim of that kidnapping was to force the release of jailed militants. Five years later, other men hijacked a plane to force the release of him.

After Kandahar, he surfaced in Pakistan. In January 2002, Daniel Pearl, a reporter for The Wall Street Journal, was kidnapped in Karachi while investigating militant networks. Pearl was killed.

A Pakistani anti-terrorism court convicted Sheikh that year and sentenced him to death. Then the case began to unravel. In 2020, a high court overturned his murder conviction. In January 2021, Pakistan's Supreme Court acquitted him. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, he was moved to a government "safe house" — under guard, but off death row.

paragraphs.text: Jaish-e-Mohammed never went away. In January 2016, attackers hit the Pathankot air base — an attack India laid at Azhar's door. Then came February 14, 2019. On the highway at Pulwama, a suicide bomber drove into a convoy of the Central Reserve Police Force. Forty personnel were killed. Jaish-e-Mohammed claimed it.

paragraphs.text: Twelve days later, Indian jets struck what India said was a Jaish-e-Mohammed training camp at Balakot, inside Pakistan. The next day, Pakistan hit back. For the second time, an attack blamed on the group Azhar founded had pulled two nuclear powers into open conflict.

Jaish-e-Mohammed never went away. In January 2016, attackers hit the Pathankot air base — an attack India laid at Azhar's door. Then came February 14, 2019. On the highway at Pulwama, a suicide bomber drove into a convoy of the Central Reserve Police Force. Forty personnel were killed. Jaish-e-Mohammed claimed it.

Twelve days later, Indian jets struck what India said was a Jaish-e-Mohammed training camp at Balakot, inside Pakistan. The next day, Pakistan hit back. In the air battle that followed, an Indian fighter was shot down and its pilot, Wing Commander Abhinandan Varthaman, was captured. He was handed back two days later. For the second time, an attack blamed on the group Azhar founded had pulled two nuclear powers into open conflict.

At the United Nations, India had spent a decade trying to list Azhar as a global terrorist. China blocked the move again and again. On May 1, 2019, it finally stepped aside. The listing came almost twenty years after the runway.
